evals.prompt: Our service saves the order to Postgres and then publishes to Kafka. Sometimes the publish fails and the event is lost. How do we fix it?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the dual write and applies the rule to never dual-write, replacing it with a transactional outbox written in the same transaction, and names the relay (poller or CDC) plus at-least-once deduplication on the consumer.

assertions.description: Names the dual write as the defect
Selects the pattern that makes write and publish atomic
Specifies how events leave the outbox

evals.prompt: Placing an order touches inventory, payments, shipping, and loyalty across four services. Two of the four external effects cannot be reversed, one team already owns the order state machine and can see every step, and another team owns three of the services. How do we coordinate it without a distributed transaction?
evals.expected_output: Chooses saga coordination from visibility, ownership, coupling and recovery needs rather than a fixed step count, and explains why the owning state machine makes orchestration the fit here while a future split would change that answer. States which effects are reversible, requires compensation to be defined before it is implemented for the reversible ones, and handles irreversible or ambiguous effects with idempotent retry, reconciliation or forward recovery. Notes that compensation is another fallible effect and applies no two-phase commit on the hot path.

value: visibility, ownership, coupling and recovery needs
rather than a fixed step count
assertions.description: Selects coordination from constraints, not a step-count rule

value: compensation to be defined before it is implemented
assertions.description: Bounds compensation to reversible effects and requires it up front

value: idempotent retry, reconciliation or forward recovery
assertions.description: Handles irreversible and ambiguous effects without pretending to compensate

evals.prompt: The team wants to rebuild our CRUD admin panel with CQRS and event sourcing because it is more scalable.
evals.expected_output: Applies no CQRS by default, separating models only after one model demonstrably fails both sides, and no event sourcing for ordinary CRUD because an audit needs an audit log; names the ongoing cost of projections, event versioning, and two models, sync lag, doubled tests.

value: only after one model demonstrably fails both sides
No event sourcing for ordinary CRUD
assertions.description: Refuses event sourcing for plain CRUD

value: Two models, sync lag, doubled tests
assertions.description: States the cost each pattern charges

evals.prompt: We have one service that writes a settings row and reads it back on the same page. The team wants CQRS with an event-sourced audit log so we are future-proof.
evals.expected_output: Applies no CQRS by default and no event sourcing for ordinary CRUD, states the constraint that would justify each, and notes that an audit needs an audit log rather than a rebuilt world.

value: No event sourcing for ordinary CRUD

assertions.description: Names the cheaper alternative and the complexity charged
Does not introduce cross-service coordination for a single-service CRUD flow

evals.prompt: A processor may commit a charge before its reply reaches us. Our worker times out, the provider does not deduplicate our reference, and a settlement file arrives nightly. The local ledger update is atomic. What must the charge path guarantee, what may happen before the next attempt, and what must we say to finance?
evals.expected_output: Treats the timeout as an unknown outcome and queries or reconciles before retrying, never retrying blindly. Keeps one stable business-operation identity across retries and replays, deduplicates delivery on a source-qualified event identity, and states that broker delivery guarantees stop at the broker. Requires settlement evidence and a named repair path before any second external effect, and tells finance the outcome is unresolved instead of claiming exactly-once across systems.

assertions.description: Names the timeout as an unknown outcome, not a failure
Separates operation identity from delivery identity
Requires evidence and an owner before a second external effect
